projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ray Davis was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Which war did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Where were you located?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Brazil, South America.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: What was your job or assignment?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: I was a clerk typist and x-ray technician.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Do you remember arriving and what it was like?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: When we arrived?

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Well, it was just an Air Force strip and the hospital was - they were just starting to build it. And it was jungle. That's about all it was to it.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Are there any memorable experiences or stories that you want to tell?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Oh. They a - all the Brazilians thought that all the Americans were rich. And that woman didn't drive cars in Brazil and they understood woman drove them in the United States and they couldn't figure that out. And they thought that the - we, well should take care of them with their charitable things. They have a lot of lepers in the area we were in and poverty was at a high level. They thought that we should donate. That was the native Brazilians did. Of course, there were some Germans there and they were just clearing them out when we got there. And there was a German air craft on the base. And they tried, the Germans tried to break the U.S. treasury that had a bunch of counterfeit American money they wanted to trade - the natives were with the Germans, some of them were - and they wanted to trade their money for this counterfeit which didn't go very good because they were to smart for them.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Is there any humorous events or things that you remember?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: In - in what part? During overseas or after we got there or?

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: It doesn't matter.

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: It doesn't matter? Oh, hell they had the hospital just about completed and another guy and I were running around in the hospital area and we looked up the corner of our eye and we saw a general coming down through the area. Well, we ducked back behind the counter, but he saw us. And he said, "don't you men know what to do when you see a general?" We stood at attention really quick. Snapped at attention. "Yes, sir."

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: What did you do to entertain yourselves?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: They had outdoor picture shows in the edge of the jungle and wrote letters. And I received a lot of mail; very fortunate. And, counted the days we get back home.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Well, the food was not to bad. We always liked to rid the cooks all the time. One time they stood up and said, "you may put your beans back in the garbage if you want to because we found worms in them." And we said, "well we both got an extra good supper tonight, so give us some more." And then they said, "you would have nuttin for supper." And we said it was goat and so we run back to the brigs and jump over the bunks and go "bah bah bah".

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Oh, you mean in the Army? Yes, I still have some of my Army buddies. Ed J.S. was at Plymouth, Indiana and we correspond and talk on the telephone and have seen each other a few times since we been back over 60 years. Well, most of them are dead is what it is. That's about it on that.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Do you recall the day that your service ended?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Sure. We - it was a Friday afternoon and I just got the last letter from Goldena that she wrote. She was a - let's see she was a CHS at that time. And they use to - on the teachers institute - which was the last of September - go to tabernacle - Indianapolis - and the choir, the CHS choir would sing with the group of others from high schools in Indiana here. And they had us all out to march. And we marched back to our barracks and somebody said that was the best job of marching they'd ever seen. We didn't have - we just - no cadence or anything. No band music, we just marched. It was a great feeling because I knew that I was going to be a civilian. Fact is, they offered me another stripe if I would stay in and another office, and I said "no", I said "I wanted to go home" and I did.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Yeah. What did you do in the weeks and days afterward?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Oh, I came home and went back to work at Krogers. Got a job right away and worked until I retired from Dolly's and 20 years ago.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: How has the service reflected your feelings on war, military in general?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Well, I feel the same way I did in '42. I went to service and I knew how the German's and the Japanese had treated the woman and children and I went to protect them and I thought that the Untied States was the best place to live and I still do that. And I'm proud that I served my country. And they wouldn't want an old man like me anymore, but I would go again if they needed me.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Yeah. Is there anything that you'd like to add that we haven't said?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Well, a quote from Johnny Wooden. He said, "that there's two people to thank in the world. One is your teacher that taught you how to read. Another one is a serviceman because when you learn to read, you learn to read in English instead of in Japanese or in German."

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Is that it?

sp.speaker: Ray Davis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ashley Janssen
sp.p: Okay.
